tagline: Paul's most personal letter: a bruised apostle defends a ministry of weakness to a church he loves, and finds God's power at work precisely there.
overview:
Second Corinthians is the most autobiographical of Paul's letters and the most emotionally exposed. It comes out of a broken relationship. After Paul wrote 1 Corinthians, things between him and the church at Corinth got worse before they got better: a visit that went badly, a letter written in tears, and then rivals who arrived with impressive credentials and questioned whether Paul was a real apostle at all. This letter is Paul's answer. He explains his changed travel plans, rejoices that the church has turned back toward him, urges them to finish their share of a relief collection for poor believers in Jerusalem, and finally confronts, with painful irony, the teachers he calls the “super-apostles” (11:5).

Running through all of it is one conviction. The gospel of a crucified Messiah produces a ministry that looks weak by the world's standards. Paul carries “this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us” (4:7). He lists his beatings, shipwrecks, and sleepless nights rather than his successes, and he reports that when he begged to be rid of a “thorn in my flesh”, the Lord answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (12:7-9).

The letter also contains some of the richest theology Paul ever wrote, almost in passing: the new covenant of the Spirit (chapter 3), the hope of the resurrection body (chapter 5), the new creation, and the ministry of reconciliation, including the great exchange of 5:21, “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” It matters because it shows what Christian leadership is supposed to look like, and it refuses the celebrity model that tempted Corinth and tempts every age.
author: The letter names Paul as its author, with Timothy as co-sender (1:1), and it is one of the letters that nearly all scholars, conservative and critical alike, accept as Paul's own. Its vocabulary, its passionate and sometimes tangled sentences, and its detailed personal history fit what we know of Paul from his other undisputed letters and from Acts. The live scholarly question is not who wrote 2 Corinthians but whether it is one letter or a collection of several Pauline letters (or letter fragments) to Corinth that were later joined together. That question is set out under the date and in the reading notes below.
date: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:8), probably around AD 53 to 55. Second Corinthians comes some months to a year or more later. Paul says he left for Troas, found no peace because Titus had not arrived, and went on to Macedonia, where Titus finally met him with good news from Corinth (2:12-13; 7:5-7). The letter, or at least chapters 1 to 9, was written from Macedonia after that meeting, most often dated around AD 55 or 56. The outer frame of Paul's chronology is anchored by an inscription found at Delphi that places Gallio's term as governor of Achaia around AD 51 to 52, during Paul's first stay in Corinth (Acts 18:12). Scholars who think chapters 10 to 13 were a separate letter date those chapters either a little before chapters 1 to 9 (if they are the tearful letter) or a little after (if they answer a fresh crisis), in either case within the same one or two years.
setting:
Corinth sat on the narrow isthmus joining mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a port on each side, and grew rich on the trade that crossed it. The old Greek city was destroyed by the Romans in 146 BC and refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC. By Paul's day it was the capital of the province of Achaia, a place of new money, ambitious freedmen, public speakers, patrons and clients, and the Isthmian games. Status mattered, and people were judged by eloquence, connections, and appearance.

The church there had a turbulent history with its founder. Paul planted it around AD 50 to 52 and stayed about eighteen months (Acts 18:11). He then wrote an earlier letter that has not survived (1 Corinthians 5:9), followed by 1 Corinthians. Later he made what he calls a “painful visit” (2:1), apparently a humiliating confrontation in which someone in the church wronged him and the church did not defend him (2:5-11; 7:12). Instead of returning as planned, he wrote a severe letter “through many tears” (2:4) and sent Titus. The church repented, and Titus brought the news. But by the time of chapters 10 to 13, other teachers had arrived. They were Jewish Christians (“Are they Hebrews? So am I,” 11:22), carried letters of recommendation (3:1), were polished speakers, accepted financial support, and mocked Paul's unimpressive presence (10:10). Scholars debate who they were: some see them as law-observant missionaries like the troublemakers in Galatia, others as Hellenistic Jewish preachers who prized visions, rhetoric, and displays of spiritual power. A minority distinguish the “super-apostles” (the Jerusalem leaders, whom rivals invoked) from the “false apostles” of 11:13; most take the two phrases to describe the same group.
purpose: Paul writes to repair and secure his relationship with the Corinthian church, and through that relationship to protect their hold on the gospel itself. He explains why he changed his travel plans and wrote a painful letter, urges the church to forgive the man who had wronged him, and rejoices in their repentance (chapters 1 to 7). He asks them to complete the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem that they had eagerly begun a year earlier (chapters 8 and 9). And he confronts the rival teachers, not by out-boasting them but by boasting in his weaknesses, so that the church will stop judging ministry by worldly standards before he arrives for a third visit (chapters 10 to 13; 12:14; 13:1).
story: Second Corinthians belongs to the period of Paul's third missionary tour, narrated in Acts 19 and 20, when he worked for more than two years in Ephesus and then passed through Macedonia and Greece. Acts 20:2-3 records that he spent three months in Greece, most likely wintering in Corinth, which suggests the reconciliation this letter hopes for largely took place. It was probably there that he wrote Romans. The collection he urges in chapters 8 and 9 was carried to Jerusalem, where Paul was arrested (Acts 21), beginning the long imprisonment that ends Acts in Rome. In the larger story of the Bible, the letter shows the new covenant promised by Jeremiah and Ezekiel coming to life in real, flawed congregations, and it ties the church's present suffering to the hope of the resurrection and the new creation.
christ: The letter's picture of Christ is shaped by the cross. Christ is the one in whom “all the promises of God are ‘Yes’” (1:20), the image of God whose glory shines in the gospel (4:4-6), and the one who, though sinless, was made sin for us so that we might become God's righteousness in him (5:21). He is the rich one who became poor for our sake (8:9), the model for Christian generosity. Above all, Paul's own life of hardship and weakness is meant to mirror the pattern of Jesus: carrying around “the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed” (4:10), and finding that Christ's power rests on him most fully when he is weak (12:9). The letter teaches that the risen Lord still works through the shape of the cross.
reading: Read 2 Corinthians as real correspondence in the middle of a painful relationship. It is not a treatise; it moves by emotion as much as by argument, doubles back, and assumes events the readers knew and we have to reconstruct. Watch for irony, especially in chapters 10 to 13, where Paul plays the fool and boasts in order to expose boasting. Don't take the list of hardships as self-pity or the “super-apostles” language as simple praise. On the letter's unity, many scholars think it joins two or more letters, most often proposing that chapters 10 to 13 were once separate (because the tone shifts so sharply from joy to confrontation), sometimes that chapters 8 and 9 were separate notes about the collection, and sometimes that 6:14-7:1 was inserted from elsewhere. Others defend the letter as a single composition, pointing out that no manuscript ever circulated in pieces and suggesting that Paul turned to the stubborn minority at the end, or that fresh news reached him while he was writing. Readers can follow the letter's argument well on either view.

structure.title: Greeting and the God of all comfort
structure.summary: Paul opens by praising God for comfort in affliction, and tells of a crushing ordeal in Asia from which God delivered him.

structure.title: Changed plans and the tearful letter
structure.summary: Paul defends his integrity in changing his travel plans, explains why he wrote instead of visiting, and urges the church to forgive the offender.

structure.title: The ministry of the new covenant
structure.summary: A long reflection on Paul's ministry: a new covenant of the Spirit, treasure in jars of clay, the hope of the resurrection body, and the message of reconciliation.

structure.title: Titus brings good news
structure.summary: Paul returns to his story: Titus met him in Macedonia with word of the church's repentance, and Paul's anguish turns to joy.

structure.title: The collection for Jerusalem
structure.summary: Paul urges the Corinthians to complete their gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem, holding up the Macedonians' generosity and the grace of Christ who became poor.

structure.title: Boasting in weakness against the super-apostles
structure.summary: Paul confronts his rivals, reluctantly boasts as a fool of hardships, visions, and a thorn in the flesh, and prepares the church for his third visit.

themes.title: Power in weakness
themes.body: The letter's central paradox is that God's power is displayed through human frailty. Paul's hardships, his unimpressive presence, and his unanswered prayer about the thorn in his flesh are not signs that he is a failed apostle but the very place where Christ's power rests on him. The Corinthians, and his rivals, wanted a leader who looked powerful. Paul insists that the pattern of the cross governs Christian ministry.

themes.title: Comfort in affliction
themes.body: The letter opens with the God of all comfort, and the word comfort runs through its early chapters. Suffering is not denied or explained away. It is shared: Christ's sufferings overflow to his people, and so does his comfort, which then passes from one believer to another. Comfort in this letter is strength to endure, not relief from trouble.

themes.title: The new covenant and new creation
themes.body: Paul describes himself as a minister of a new covenant, written by the Spirit on human hearts rather than on stone tablets (chapter 3), echoing the promises of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Those who are in Christ belong to a new creation (5:17), and God has given them a ministry of reconciliation that reaches out to the world.

themes.title: Generosity as grace
themes.body: Chapters 8 and 9 treat giving as a work of God's grace in people, not a tax or a fundraising scheme. The model is Christ, who became poor so that others might become rich. Paul stresses willingness, fairness between churches, and scrupulous honesty in handling money, and he sees the gift as a bond of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers.

themes.title: What makes a true ministry
themes.body: Against rivals who measured leaders by eloquence, letters of recommendation, pay, and spiritual experiences, Paul offers a different test: sincerity before God, the changed lives of the people served, faithfulness to the gospel of the crucified Christ, and a willingness to suffer for others. His own converts, he says, are his letter of recommendation.

keyChapters.why: The God of all comfort, Paul's near-death ordeal in Asia, and the declaration that every promise of God is Yes in Christ.
The ministry of the new covenant, written by the Spirit, and the unveiled faces that are being transformed into the Lord's image.
Treasure in jars of clay: the light of God's glory in the face of Christ carried by fragile, afflicted messengers.
The hope of the resurrection body, the new creation, and the ministry of reconciliation grounded in the great exchange of 5:21.
The grace of giving, modeled on Christ who though rich became poor, and the collection for the believers in Jerusalem.
Paul's vision of the third heaven, the thorn in his flesh, and the Lord's answer that his power is perfected in weakness.
